title: Should You Clean Your Air Ducts After a Remodel?
h1: Should You Clean Your Air Ducts After a Remodel?
description: Should you clean air ducts after a remodel? How construction dust gets into ducts, the signs it is there, and how to protect your HVAC system during the work.
quick_answer: Yes, in most cases. Drywall dust, sawdust and plaster get pulled into return vents during a remodel and settle in the ducts, filter, blower and coil. If the system ran during the work or vents weren't sealed, a duct cleaning afterward keeps that fine dust from blowing around your new space for months.
body:
How does construction dust get into air ducts?

During a remodel, sanding drywall, cutting wood and demolishing old materials put a lot of fine dust in the air. If the HVAC system runs, the return vents pull that dust straight in. Some is caught by the filter, but fine drywall dust clogs filters fast, then slips past and coats the blower, the coil and the inside of the ducts.

Even with the system off, dust settles into open supply vents and return grilles. When the system starts again, it blows that dust back out into your freshly finished rooms.

What are the signs of construction dust in your ducts?

  • A fine white or gray dust settling on surfaces soon after you clean
  • Dust puffing out of vents when the system starts
  • A filter that clogs within days or weeks of the project ending
  • Visible dust or debris when you remove a vent cover
  • Reduced airflow from some vents
  • A dusty or burnt smell when the heat first runs

If your project involved drywall work, flooring removal or demolition, it's safe to assume some dust got in.

Why is drywall dust hard on HVAC systems?

Drywall dust is very fine. It loads filters quickly, which restricts airflow and makes the blower work harder. Dust that gets past the filter sticks to the blower wheel and indoor coil, which lowers efficiency and can lead to freezing or overheating. In furnaces, dust on the heat exchanger and components can cause odors and nuisance problems.

For people with allergies or asthma, construction dust circulating through the house is a common source of irritation in the weeks after a project.

How can you protect your HVAC system during a remodel?

If the project hasn't started yet, a little planning saves a lot of cleanup:

  1. Turn the system off during dusty work whenever the weather allows. Most of the year in coastal San Diego and Orange County, that's easy.
  2. Seal vents and returns in the work area with plastic and painter's tape.
  3. Use a cheap filter during construction and change it often, then install a good filter when the project ends.
  4. Set up dust barriers with plastic sheeting and zippered doors to keep dust in the work zone.
  5. Ask the crew to use dust collection on sanders and saws.

If you need cooling during a hot inland summer, change the filter every few days during dusty phases rather than letting it clog.

Does it matter what kind of remodel you did?

Some projects are harder on ducts than others. Drywall sanding, plaster repair, tearing out old flooring and demolition make the finest and most persistent dust. A kitchen or bathroom remodel near a return grille is a common culprit. Projects in older homes can also disturb materials like old popcorn ceiling, so if those were involved, make sure they were tested and handled properly before any cleanup begins.

Painting alone, done with the system off, usually puts much less into the ducts.

When should you clean ducts after a remodel?

Wait until all the dusty work is finished, including drywall sanding, painting prep and flooring. Cleaning in the middle of a project just gives the dust a fresh place to land. Once the work is done and the house has been cleaned, schedule the duct cleaning before you move furniture back or settle into the new space.

A thorough post-construction cleaning covers all supply and return runs, registers and grilles, the blower area and a check of the coil. The technician should also look for ducts that were crushed, disconnected or cut during the work.

What else should be checked after a remodel?

  • That vents in new or moved rooms are connected and blowing properly
  • That the system airflow suits any added square footage
  • That attic ducts weren't stepped on or disconnected by other trades
  • That new walls or cabinets didn't block a return grille
  • That the dryer vent wasn't kinked or crushed if laundry areas were moved

Our air duct cleaning includes a post-construction inspection so you know the system is clean and connected properly before you settle back in.
faqs: How long after a remodel should I wait to clean my ducts?

Schedule it after all dusty work is finished, including drywall sanding, demolition and flooring, and after the house has been cleaned. That way dust from the final stages doesn't end up in freshly cleaned ducts.
Can I just change the filter instead of cleaning the ducts?

Changing the filter is the first step and you should do it right away. It won't remove dust that already got past the filter into the ducts, blower and coil. If you still see dust coming from vents after a filter change, the ducts need cleaning.
Should I run my AC during a remodel?

Avoid running it during dusty phases if you can. If you need it, seal the vents and returns in the work area and change the filter every few days. A clogged filter can strain the system and lets fine dust slip past.
Does a small remodel need duct cleaning?

Not always. A quick paint job with the system off and vents covered may not put much dust in the ducts. Look behind a return grille and check the filter. If you see fine white dust, a cleaning is worth it.
